newsitem.title: Netherlands: FOCUS-DE BOER, UNIGRO MERGE, RESTRUCTURE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DE BOER, UNIGRO MERGE, RESTRUCTURE.

text.p: Food wholesaling and supermarket groups De Boer Winkelbedrijven NV and unlisted Unigro on Tuesday unveiled details of the merger which will propel them to the number two slot in the Dutch grocery sector after Ahold NV .

The deal, finalised on May 2 subject to shareholders' approval and retroactive to January 1 this year, will create a combine with annual turnover of more than six billion guilders ($3.1 billion). The merger was announced in October.
Investors cheered the combine's announcement of a five-for-two stock split and its solid earnings prospects, initially sending De Boer shares 10 guilders higher to 161.00.
Shares later settled at 158.50, up nearly 5.5 percent.
The new combine will have a market share of 13 percent in the Netherlands, second to the 28 percent commanded by giant Ahold's Albert Heijn supermarket subsidiary.
It is a member of the biggest Dutch purchasing combine Superunie which has a market share of 30 percent.
"Together with our Superunie friends, we'll have a very strong strategic purchasing position," Robert ter Haar, chairman of De Boer Unigro, told a news conference.
The deal creates a merged group with annual turnover of more than six billion guilders.
Ter Haar said De Boer Unigro's activities would be grouped into six business units which would share certain service departments, generating major financial synergies.
"We didn't merge for the sake of cost reduction. We want to build a new, strong company, which will, eventually, lead to cost reductions," he said.

In the Netherlands, the combine will restructure to boost efficiency, shedding an estimated 250-300 jobs, and closing four distribution centres over the next three years. The two companies combined currently employ 10,000 people.
The restructuring will be financed by a 72 million guilder provision to be charged to De Boer Unigro shareholders' equity.
The new group will operate two flagship chains in the Netherlands, combining a string of large Super De Boer supermarkets with smaller local Spar convenience stores.

In Belgium the combine also operates a Spar chain and in Spain it owns Super El Arbol supermarkets, where annual turnover is targeted to double to 2.5 billion guilders within five years through both organic growth and acquisitions.
"There are great opportunities in Spain, where the market is still much more fragmented than over here," Ter Haar said.
In contrast to the 30 percent market share controlled by Dutch number one Ahold, Spain's leading players commanded no more than six to seven percent of the market each, he said.
"It's also much easier to open new shops in Spain," he said.
The combine said it saw a "clear increase" in net profits per share in 1997, and was targeting average long-term net earnings growth of ten percent annually.
The combine's pro-forma net profit for 1996 amounted to 90.1 million guilders or 8.48 guilders per share on combined turnover of 6.4 billion guilders, the companies said.
The combine will maintain De Boer's dividend policy of an average 35 percent pay-out from ordinary profits after tax.
In 1996/97 Unigro posted net profits of 32.2 million guilders on turnover of 4.25 billion.
De Boer was smaller but more profitable with a 1996 net profit of 35.2 million guilders on turnover of 2.11 billion.
The firms said they planned a five-for-two stock split after the merger, which will be effected by means of a share swap.

Under the terms of the merger all Unigro shares will transferred to De Boer, which will subsequently place 6.05 million new shares plus one million warrants with Unigro's original shareholder, it said.
After the merger, the Unigro holding company will own some 57 percent of outstanding De Boer Unigro shares, which it will reduce to 49.9 percent at most within six months.
Analysts said the details were largely as expected, with some characterising the earnings forecast as modest.

"There are no really big surprises in the news. Most of the steps that were announced are a logical consequence of the merger, and I think profit growth can easily outstrip the forecast that's been given," said Dennis Jullens of ING Barings.
"I think it's mainly relief the merger is now 100 percent sure which is pushing up the shares," Jullens said, adding the stock was still relatively undervalued.
By Christine Lucassen- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
